old: Ampere's circuital law states that the line integral of $\vec{B}$ around any closed loop equals $\mu_0$ times the net current enclosed by that loop. It is useful only when symmetry makes B constant along a chosen path. For an infinitely long straight wire, take a circle of radius r around the wire, which gives $B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$; the field lines are concentric circles. Inside a solid wire carrying uniform current, B grows linearly with r. Outside the wire it falls as 1/r, and it is maximum at the surface. For a long solid wire, a rectangular Amperian loop gives a uniform field $B=\mu_0 nI$ inside, where n is the number of turns per unit length. The field outside is nearly zero. At either end of a long solenoid the field is half the central value. A toroid, which is a solenoid bent into a ring, has $B=\frac{\mu_0 NI}{2\pi r}$ inside its core and zero field both in the open space and outside.
